title: Atmospheric perspective — Image Wiki
text:
Atmospheric perspective
  Distant things go pale, flat and sky-coloured because you are looking at them through more air, and air scatters light.

  
    Termatmospheric perspective
    Also calledaerial perspective, depth haze, atmospheric haze
    Not the same aslinear perspective, depth of field, low contrast
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Why it happens"Distant things go blue" is only sometimes trueHow much air it takesWhat you can see in the pictureAcross different mediaCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Find a window with something far away in it — a ridge of hills, a row of tower blocks across a city. The near ones are dark and you can pick out windows and trees on them. The far ones are pale, almost flat, and close to the colour of the sky. If several ridges sit behind each other you can count them, because each is a shade lighter than the one in front.
Nobody arranged that. It is what air does to light. Smarthistory puts it in one line: as we look into the distance we lose visual clarity, and the specificity of colour decreases too. The name for it is atmospheric perspective, or aerial perspective — Tate and Smarthistory use the two interchangeably. It is the depth cue that works when there are no straight lines to converge: Linear perspective needs architecture, and for a valley or a coastline this is what you have.
Why it happens
Two things happen to light in the column of air between you and that mountain. Some of the light leaving the mountain is scattered sideways out of the beam before it reaches you, so it arrives dimmer. And some skylight that was never going to reach you is scattered into the beam from the side, adding a veil of sky-coloured light on top of the picture. The second part is the one that matters, because the amount added does not care what it lands on: a dark cliff and a bright snowfield at the same distance receive the same veil.
Adding a constant amount of light to everything does four things at once.
Contrast collapses. Say the dark rock sends you 5 units of light and the snow 80 — a ratio of 16 to 1. Add 40 units of veil to each and you have 45 and 120, a ratio of 2.7 to 1. Nothing was subtracted; contrast fell because the gap between them stayed the same size while both numbers grew.
Everything gets lighter, and the darks go first. In that arithmetic the rock got nine times brighter and the snow one and a half times. Shadow detail is the first casualty of distance, which is why a distant hillside loses its shadows before it loses its shape.
Colour drains toward the colour of the air. The veil carries its own colour and dilutes whatever came off the object. A green forest at 20 kilometres is a blue-grey silhouette shaped like a forest.
Fine detail goes — and mostly because contrast went. A crack in a rock face reaches you as a small local difference in brightness; crush all differences by a factor of six and it drops below what your eye can find.
Why blue, in the usual case: short wavelengths scatter more strongly in clean air, so the light the sky scatters at you is blue, and so is the veil.



Ansel Adams, Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, between 1933 and 1942. National Archives. Public domain, US government work.
That arithmetic in one frame, in black and white, so no colour distracts you. Rank four things by how dark their darkest part is: the butte filling the foreground has true blacks and countable rubble; the walls across the middle are mid-grey with the rock banding still readable; the far rim is a flat light band; the mountains on the skyline are barely a shade darker than the sky.
Note the order things were lost in. Shadow detail went first — the far rim has shape but no shadows in it — and the fine detail followed because the contrast carrying it went. Nothing here is blue, and the cue is at full strength.


"Distant things go blue" is only sometimes true
Taught as a rule, that sentence will make you mark correct images wrong. The veil takes the colour of whatever the air happens to be scattering at you: pale blue in clean dry air, orange or gold under a low sun or in dust and smoke, neutral white in fog, yellow-brown in heavy smog.


Clean dry air: a blue veil spent over tens of kilometres
Fog: a white veil spent over about a hundred metres


Left: Gaurav Kapatia, hills at Chopta, Uttarakhand, CC BY-SA 4.0. Right: Dietmar Rabich, trees in fog near Dülmen, CC BY-SA 4.0. Two air masses, one cue.
Left, clean mountain air. The ridge on the right is dark green with individual conifers you can pick out; behind it four or five more ridges climb toward the horizon, each paler, bluer and flatter than the last, until one is barely separable from the sky. The sky does it too — deepest at the top of the frame, palest at the horizon, because a horizontal line of sight goes through far more air than an upward one.
Right, a farm track in fog, with trees of the same kind and size along it. The nearest is brown-black with countable twigs, the next is already a grey outline, and within four or five the row has dissolved into white. Same ladder, spent over about a hundred metres instead of tens of kilometres, because this air is carrying vastly more water — and the veil is white, not blue. Check the sky in the picture first, then check whether the far things are heading toward it.


How much air it takes
Strength is path length multiplied by how much the air is carrying, so the same cue operates over wildly different scales: ten kilometres in cold dry mountain air, a few hundred metres in dust or humidity, fifty in fog, one room with a haze machine.



Change this
What happens




More distance
Paler, flatter, less saturated, softer — all together


Cleaner, drier, colder air
The effect stretches out over a longer distance


Humidity, dust, smoke, smog
Compresses to hundreds of metres, and the veil changes colour


Looking toward the sun
Much stronger — scattering is strongest in the forward direction, so the same hill washes out into the light and keeps its bite with the sun behind you



What you can see in the picture

Blacks stop being black. Nothing in the far distance is as dark as the darkest thing in the foreground. The most reliable single sign, and the easiest to check.
Edges lose bite without going soft. A distant treeline becomes a low-contrast grey band with a still-crisp outline.




Albert Bierstadt, Among the Sierra Nevada, California, 1868, public domain.
The same ladder built by hand, in colour. The trees on the right bank are green and near-black in their shadows, with branches you could count; the slopes in the middle distance have lost most of their green; the peaks at the back are a narrow band of light values with no nameable detail. Compare the darkest spot in those peaks with the darkest spot in the foreground trees — the mountains never come close. Distance is not pushing them toward black, it is pushing them toward the sky, and once two things reach the same value the boundary between them disappears.
The veil here is warm, not blue: the light breaking through the cloud is golden, and haze takes the colour of the light it scatters.


Across different media

Painting. Perugino graded a whole fresco this way — bold colour on the foreground figures, paler ones in the middle ground, hills fading to pale blue at the back (it is reproduced in Depth cues). Smarthistory makes the sharp point about what changed in the Renaissance: instead of painting what they knew a distant mountain looked like, painters began painting the visual phenomenon, which is a mountain gone pale.
Photography. You get it whether you want it or not. Overdone dehaze is the familiar failure — the far ridges come back to full contrast and the picture goes flat, because the depth cue has been deleted.
3D and CG. Usually a separate "fog" or depth-fade setting. Leave it off and a valley ten kilometres wide renders as a tabletop model.

Common mistakes

"Distant things go blue." Only in clean air. The veil is the colour of the air, and the sky in the same picture tells you which.
"It's a Renaissance convention." It is photometry. Photographs do it with no artist involved — one of the few things in this wiki that is not a matter of taste.
"Haze is the same as blur." Haze lowers contrast and leaves the edges where they were, so a hazy ridge has a sharp but faint outline. Blur spreads edges out and can stay high contrast while doing it. See Depth of field.
"Add haze to make it look deep." Only if it increases with distance. A uniform grey wash over the frame is just a washed-out picture.
"Landscapes only." A long corridor, a cathedral interior, a smoke-filled room. Any air in the way counts.


The monotonic test

Rank three or four objects front to back by overlap alone. That is your true depth order — see Depth cues.
Rank them again by contrast (how dark is the darkest part of each?) and by saturation.
Both rankings must match the first, and the change must be gradual. Patchy haze is the tell — two things at the same depth, one crisp and one washed out, cannot both be right.
Compare the darkest point of the far distance with the darkest point of the foreground. If the mountain contains a true black, either there is no air in this picture or the mountain is not far away.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Depth cues
              A picture is a flat surface. It reads as deep because a dozen separate cues all point the same way, and your eye believes the majority.
            
          
        
          
            
              Linear perspective
              Parallel lines in the world meet at a point in the picture, because equal real distances take up less of your view the further away they are.
            
          
        
          
            
              Value structure
              How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.
            
          
        
          
            
              The colour of the light
              What you see is the object's own colour multiplied by the light's colour — and your brain quietly divides the light back out, which is why a white shirt looks white everywhere.
